title: Mapping Every Contact, Slice by Slice
endLine: Serial slices map every contact; proving synapses and function takes more.

scenes.tts: How do you map every neuron in a piece of brain? In the inner retina, amacrine cells tangle with ganglion cells, the retina's output neurons. A single slice shows only flat patches where branches cross the cut. To trace who meets whom, you must reconstruct the whole volume.

scenes.visual: A large translucent schematic block of mouse inner retina fills most of the frame height, drifting slowly. Inside, tangled glowing branches of amacrine cells and output ganglion cells appear as the question is asked. A cutting plane sweeps across the block and slides out a single flat slice to the side, turning the branches into scattered flat patches; the patches then pull back into the full translucent volume.

scenes.tts: Serial block-face electron microscopy builds that volume step by step. Start with a small block of mouse retina. The microscope captures an electron micrograph of the flat top face. Then a thin slice is shaved away, exposing a fresh face below. Repeating this cycle creates a stack of consecutive micrographs.

scenes.visual: Carry the same schematic mouse retina block in place. A scanning beam sweeps across its flat top face; a matching greyscale electron micrograph (labelled 'schematic') peels off to the right. Next, the thin top layer is shaved away and vanishes, exposing a fresh face below. The scan-and-shave cycle repeats smoothly, lowering the block while building a stack of consecutive micrographs beside it.

scenes.tts: Those flat images still have to become whole cells. Researchers trace each branch's outline across consecutive slices, combining manual tracing with machine-learning segmentation, software that outlines cells automatically. Stacking those outlines rebuilds each neuron's branching tree, its arbor. Where reconstructed membranes meet, the map marks a contact. Together, the reconstructed neurons and chemical synapses form a connectome.

scenes.visual: Carry the stack of schematic micrographs on the left and open volume space on the right. A bright contour outlines one cell slice by slice (label: 'manual tracing'), then surrounding profiles fill in with distinct colours in parallel (label: 'machine-learning segmentation'). The coloured outlines extrude out of the stack and fuse into branching neuron arbors (label: 'arbor'). Bright dots appear where membranes press together (label: 'contact'), forming a glowing schematic connectome.

scenes.tts: Now pause and look at one reconstructed branch meeting two neighbouring ganglion cells. One partner gets many contacts, while the neighbour gets far fewer. Does a larger count prove a stronger synapse, or even prove every contact is a synapse?
scenes.caption: Now pause and look at one reconstructed branch meeting two neighbouring ganglion cells. One partner gets many contacts, while the neighbour gets far fewer. Does a larger count prove a stronger synapse, or even prove every contact is a synapse?
scenes.visual: Zoom smoothly into the same reconstructed retinal volume (schematic), focusing on one starburst amacrine branch meeting two neighbouring ganglion cells. Many bright contact dots light up along the left ganglion cell (label: 'many contacts') and only a few along the right ganglion cell (label: 'few contacts'). High-contrast question text appears above: 'More contacts = stronger synapse?'

scenes.visual: Hold the zoomed-in reconstructed branch and two ganglion cells (schematic) with 'More contacts = stronger synapse?' on screen at full contrast. Keep a gentle ambient pulse on the contact dots throughout the thinking pause.

scenes.tts: No. Serial slices reconstruct cells and contacts, yet a contact alone cannot prove a synapse, and anatomy alone cannot prove function. Packed branches can touch without signalling, so a contact map proposes partners and does not prove them. A connectome also counts synapses without measuring strength or sign, meaning excitation or inhibition. Treating count as strength is an assumption.

scenes.visual: Transform the same zoomed-in contact scene (schematic). First, several contact dots fade into hollow dashed rings beside the label 'contact ≠ proven synapse'. Next, a schematic tally counts the remaining chemical synapses (label: 'synapse count'), while two paired schematic gauges beside it — 'strength' and 'sign (excite / inhibit)' — stay dimmed with question marks.

scenes.tts: Nor can a wiring diagram alone say which direction a ganglion cell prefers. To guard against that limit, experimenters read function first. They image calcium in the retina, using moving bars to read each cell's preferred direction. Then they cut and reconstruct that same tissue. Still, anatomy only observes; proving a pathway is needed takes a manipulation.

scenes.visual: Pull back to the same schematic mouse retina block, rewound intact before slicing. A bright moving bar sweeps repeatedly across the retina while ganglion cells flash with schematic calcium glow; a crisp directional arrow locks onto each cell (label: 'read function first'). The exact same labelled block then slices down and reconstructs its branches with each cell's arrow preserved. Finish with a clean tag: 'observational: need takes manipulation'.

scenes.tts: This approach unlocked real circuits. Briggman, Helmstaedter and Denk imaged calcium using moving bars in wild-type mouse retina. They then cut that same tissue to reconstruct direction-selective ganglion cells and their contacts. In 2013, Helmstaedter and colleagues paired manual tracing with machine-learning segmentation. They reconstructed nine hundred and fifty neurons and their mutual contacts in the mouse retina.

First spotlight a direction-selective ganglion cell with its moving-bar arrow and its reconstructed contacts (schematic; no wiring result drawn), tagged 'Briggman, Helmstaedter & Denk'. Then zoom out across the wider mouse retina volume as dense colourful branches populate the block, with a schematic counter rising to '950 neurons' and tag 'Helmstaedter and colleagues, 2013'.

scenes.tts: In 2018, Bae and colleagues used electron microscopy on a retinal patch whose light responses were imaged. Grouping cells by arbor shape and depth in the inner retina revealed forty-seven anatomical clusters and at least thirty-five types. A stack of slices maps who meets whom, while activity and manipulations reveal what each circuit does.
